pmr.group.right-hand.name: Right Hand & Forearm
pmr.group.right-hand.tenseCue: Make a tight fist, squeeze hard, and feel the tension in your fingers and forearm.
pmr.group.right-hand.releaseCue: Open your hand, let it go completely limp, and feel your fingers relax.
pmr.group.left-hand.name: Left Hand & Forearm
pmr.group.left-hand.tenseCue: Make a tight fist, squeeze hard, and feel the tension in your fingers and forearm.
pmr.group.left-hand.releaseCue: Open your hand, let it go completely limp, and notice the warm, heavy feeling.
pmr.group.right-arm.name: Right Upper Arm
pmr.group.right-arm.tenseCue: Bend your elbow, flex your bicep hard, and feel the muscle bulge.
pmr.group.right-arm.releaseCue: Lower your arm to your side, let the muscle go soft, and feel the heaviness.
pmr.group.left-arm.name: Left Upper Arm
pmr.group.left-arm.tenseCue: Bend your elbow, flex your bicep hard, and feel the strength.
pmr.group.left-arm.releaseCue: Lower your arm to your side, let tension drain away, and feel the heaviness.
pmr.group.forehead.name: Forehead & Scalp
pmr.group.forehead.tenseCue: Raise your eyebrows high, wrinkle your forehead, and feel the tension across your scalp.
pmr.group.forehead.releaseCue: Let your eyebrows drop naturally, smooth out your forehead, and feel your skin relax.
pmr.group.face.name: Eyes & Nose
pmr.group.face.tenseCue: Squeeze your eyes tight, scrunch your nose up, and scrunch your whole face together.
pmr.group.face.releaseCue: Let your face go soft, eyes gently closed, nose and cheeks smooth and relaxed.
pmr.group.jaw.name: Mouth & Jaw
pmr.group.jaw.tenseCue: Bite down hard, clench your teeth, and feel your jaw muscles working.
pmr.group.jaw.releaseCue: Let your jaw drop slightly open, lips barely touching, and tongue resting softly.
pmr.group.neck.name: Neck & Throat
pmr.group.neck.tenseCue: Draw the chin in slightly and tighten the neck.
pmr.group.neck.releaseCue: Let your head find its natural position, neck long and loose, and throat open.
pmr.group.shoulders.name: Shoulders
pmr.group.shoulders.tenseCue: Pull your shoulders up high toward your ears and feel the squeeze in your upper back.
pmr.group.shoulders.releaseCue: Let your shoulders drop naturally, feeling them sink lower, heavy and loose.
pmr.group.upper-back.name: Upper Back & Chest
pmr.group.upper-back.tenseCue: Squeeze your shoulder blades together, arch your back slightly, and expand your chest.
pmr.group.upper-back.releaseCue: Let your back settle naturally, shoulder blades apart, and chest soft and open.
pmr.group.abdomen.name: Abdomen
pmr.group.abdomen.tenseCue: Tighten your abs hard, pull your belly button in, and make your stomach firm.
pmr.group.abdomen.releaseCue: Let your stomach go soft, breathe into your belly, and feel it rise and fall naturally.
pmr.group.lower-back.name: Lower Back
pmr.group.lower-back.tenseCue: Gently arch the lower back. Stop if it hurts.
pmr.group.lower-back.releaseCue: Let your back settle to its natural curve, supported, comfortable, and loose.
pmr.group.hips.name: Hips & Buttocks
pmr.group.hips.tenseCue: Squeeze your buttocks together hard, clench tight, and feel tension in your hips.
pmr.group.hips.releaseCue: Let your muscles go soft, feeling them spread naturally, heavy and relaxed.
pmr.group.right-thigh.name: Right Thigh
pmr.group.right-thigh.tenseCue: Straighten your right leg, flex your thigh muscle hard, and feel it firm and strong.
pmr.group.right-thigh.releaseCue: Let your leg rest naturally, thigh muscle soft, loose, heavy, and comfortable.
pmr.group.left-thigh.name: Left Thigh
pmr.group.left-thigh.tenseCue: Straighten your left leg, flex your thigh muscle hard, and feel the strength.
pmr.group.left-thigh.releaseCue: Let your leg rest naturally, thigh completely relaxed, and notice the contrast.
pmr.group.right-calf.name: Right Calf & Shin
pmr.group.right-calf.tenseCue: Point your foot down hard, then flex toes up toward your shin, feeling both sides work.
pmr.group.right-calf.releaseCue: Let your foot rest naturally, calf and shin completely loose and soft.
pmr.group.left-calf.name: Left Calf & Shin
pmr.group.left-calf.tenseCue: Point your foot down hard, then flex toes up toward your shin, feeling muscles engage.
pmr.group.left-calf.releaseCue: Let your foot rest naturally, all lower leg muscles relaxed and heavy.
pmr.group.right-foot.name: Right Foot
pmr.group.right-foot.tenseCue: Curl your toes down tight, scrunch them up, and feel tension in your foot arch.
pmr.group.right-foot.releaseCue: Let your toes uncurl naturally, foot completely soft, warm, and relaxed.
pmr.group.left-foot.name: Left Foot
pmr.group.left-foot.tenseCue: Curl your toes down tight, scrunch them up, and feel your arch working.
pmr.group.left-foot.releaseCue: Let your toes spread naturally, foot loose and relaxed, and all tension gone.
pmr.info.intro: Progressive muscle relaxation systematically releases physical tension throughout the body. Tense each muscle group firmly for 10 seconds, then release completely for 10 seconds to feel the contrast.
pmr.info.how.heading: How it works
pmr.info.how.body: Progressive muscle relaxation teaches your body the contrast between tension and relaxation. Deliberately tensing a muscle group and releasing it activates the parasympathetic nervous system, lowering heart rate and releasing built-up physical stress.
pmr.info.how.card1.title: Tension contrast
pmr.info.how.card1.body: Deliberately tensing muscles makes the subsequent release more noticeable and effective, releasing tension held without realizing it.
pmr.info.how.card2.title: Nervous system shift
pmr.info.how.card2.body: Releasing muscle tension triggers parasympathetic activation, slowing your heart rate and diminishing stress hormones.
pmr.info.how.card3.title: Body awareness
pmr.info.how.card3.body: Regular practice trains you to recognize physical tension earlier and release stress before it accumulates throughout your day.
pmr.info.science.heading: The science
pmr.info.science.body: Clinical trials show that progressive muscle relaxation produces significant, sustained reductions in anxiety across diverse settings, from high-stress hospital environments to academic performance.
pmr.info.science.card1.title: Clinical anxiety reduction
pmr.info.science.card1.body: A randomized trial found 30 minutes of daily progressive muscle relaxation over 5 days lowered anxiety scores by 22% compared to controls.
pmr.info.science.card2.title: Demanding environments
pmr.info.science.card2.body: In a randomized trial among 46 nurses, progressive muscle relaxation reduced anxiety on the DASS-21 with a large effect size (Cohen's d=1.61).
pmr.info.science.card3.title: Clinical training
pmr.info.science.card3.body: In 90 nursing students during clinical training, five 45-minute sessions reduced State-Trait Anxiety Inventory scores from 55 to 24.4 (a 56% decrease).
pmr.info.when.heading: When to practice
pmr.info.when.item1: When you notice physical tension building in shoulders, jaw, or back
pmr.info.when.item2: Before stressful events to release anticipatory tension
pmr.info.when.item3: At the end of your workday to transition into relaxation
pmr.info.when.item4: Before bed to release tension interfering with sleep
pmr.info.notice.heading: What you'll notice
pmr.info.notice.item1: Immediate awareness of tension you didn't realize you were holding
pmr.info.notice.item2: A deep sensation of warmth and heaviness as muscles release
pmr.info.notice.item3: Slower breathing and a calmer baseline heart rate
pmr.info.notice.item4: Faster ability to spot and release physical stress throughout the day
pmr.info.tips.heading: Tips for best results
pmr.info.tips.card1.title: Comfortable position
pmr.info.tips.card1.body: Sit in a supportive armchair or lie down comfortably. Loosen any tight clothing so your body is fully supported.
pmr.info.tips.card2.title: Gentle firmness
pmr.info.tips.card2.body: Tense each muscle firmly but never to the point of pain or cramping. The goal is clear sensation, not strain.
pmr.info.tips.card3.title: Notice the contrast
pmr.info.tips.card3.body: Focus your full attention on the difference between the tensed state and the limp release that follows.
pmr.info.disclaimer: This is a tension-and-release practice for everyday calm. It is not therapy and does not treat anxiety disorders or any medical condition. Tense firmly, not to the point of pain or cramping. If a movement hurts, skip that group. Stop if you feel dizzy or unwell.
info.intro: A short, guided breathing practice. Follow the orb: it grows as you breathe in and settles as you breathe out. You don't need to read any of this to start — it will be here whenever you're curious.
info.how.heading: How it works
info.how.body:
The 4:6 rhythm makes every exhale longer than the inhale. That long, slow out-breath stimulates the vagus nerve — the main pathway of the parasympathetic nervous system — signalling the body to shift from "fight or flight" into "rest and repair".

The shift is measurable: heart rate slows, blood pressure eases, and circulation improves, bringing more oxygen to the brain. Practised regularly, it becomes a reliable lever you can pull whenever stress builds.
info.how.card1.title: Vagal nerve activation
info.how.card1.body: Slow, deep breathing stimulates the vagus nerve, which connects the brain to the heart and digestive system and promotes a calm state.
info.how.card2.title: Optimal gas exchange
info.how.card2.body: Breathing at 4–6 breaths per minute optimizes oxygen delivery and CO₂ balance, countering the shallow over-breathing that often comes with anxiety.
info.how.card3.title: Lower stress hormones
info.how.card3.body: Regular practice reduces cortisol and other stress hormones, improving the body's baseline stress response over time.
info.science.heading: The science
info.science.body: Research consistently shows that slow, diaphragmatic breathing produces measurable reductions in anxiety, stress hormones, and physiological arousal. In one controlled study, an 8-week program of 15-minute sessions lowered negative affect and significantly decreased cortisol levels in healthy adults.
info.science.card1.title: Anxiety reduction
info.science.card1.body: Five days of guided deep breathing (15–20 minutes, four times daily) reduced anxiety scores in hospitalized patients by 43%, while a control group showed no change.
info.science.card2.title: Panic disorder
info.science.card2.body: A review of 16 studies found that slow-breathing training over 2–12 months reduced panic attack frequency and normalized CO₂ levels in panic disorder and agoraphobia.
info.science.card3.title: Generalized anxiety
info.science.card3.body: Three months of daily breathing practice reduced anxiety scores by 68% in a study of 41 people with generalized anxiety disorder.
info.when.heading: When to practice
info.when.item1: When you feel overwhelmed or stressed
info.when.item4: After stressful events, to reset your nervous system
info.notice.heading: What you'll notice
info.notice.item1: A calming effect within the first minute
info.notice.item3: A slower heart rate and softer muscle tension
info.notice.item4: Better stress resilience with regular practice
info.tips.heading: Tips for best results
info.tips.card1.title: Posture
info.tips.card1.body: Sit or stand tall so the lungs can expand fully. Keep the shoulders heavy and relaxed, not hunched.
info.tips.card2.title: Environment
info.tips.card2.body: Choose a quiet spot where you won't be interrupted. A comfortable temperature makes it easier to stay with the breath.
info.tips.card3.title: Consistency
info.tips.card3.body: Practice the same rhythm for a week before changing anything. Familiarity is what makes it work under real stress.
info.disclaimer: These exercises support everyday calm. They are not therapy and do not treat anxiety disorders or any medical condition. If a breathing exercise ever feels uncomfortable or makes you dizzy, stop and let your breath return to normal.
